caveats: Multiplatform native targets require target-specific toolchains (e.g. Kotlin/Native compiler backends), which is a portability/dependency trade-off scored here as a moderate rather than maximal simplicity score.
metric.dependency_simplicity.method: Static review of Kotlin language/toolchain dependency semantics using programs under template/programs/kotlin/micro and adversarial as representative workload sources; no external native library or SIMD outsourcing observed in reviewed sources.
observations: Kotlin standard library (kotlin-stdlib) is the only mandatory runtime dependency for JVM targets; it is small, versioned in lockstep with the compiler, and distributed alongside the compiler release.
Kotlin/JVM programs additionally require the JVM runtime (JRE) as a platform dependency; this is an implicit but well-defined, single, stable dependency rather than a sprawling dependency graph.

Compiling and running the reviewed micro-benchmarks (mb00-mb11) requires only 'kotlinc' plus a JVM; no third-party libraries, package manager resolution, or build-tool plugin ecosystem is needed for these representative single-file programs.

Kotlin Multiplatform / Kotlin/Native introduces additional per-target runtime pieces (native memory model, platform libs) which adds some complexity beyond the pure JVM path, slightly reducing simplicity relative to single-runtime languages.

Gradle/Maven are conventional for larger projects but are not intrinsically required by the language for the reviewed program scale; this keeps the dependency footprint of the language itself simple, distinct from ecosystem-level package manager maturity (out of scope here).
No evidence in the reviewed sources of hidden transitive dependency bloat introduced by the language itself; kotlin-stdlib has effectively zero external dependencies.

caveats: Realized breadth of currently-supported platforms/targets and their maturity is an Ecosystem concern and is intentionally excluded from this Language Quality score.
metric.portability_design_platform_neutr.method: Static review of Kotlin's language-level platform-neutrality design (JVM/JS/Native compilation targets, expect/actual mechanism) as evidenced by general language design and the absence of platform-specific constructs in reviewed micro programs.
observations: Kotlin is designed as a multiplatform language: the same source can target JVM bytecode, JavaScript, and native binaries via Kotlin/Native (LLVM-based), with 'expect/actual' declarations providing a first-class mechanism for platform-specific implementations behind a common API.

Reviewed micro-benchmark programs (mb00-mb11) use only core language constructs and kotlin-stdlib APIs, with no OS-specific syscalls, file-system path assumptions, or platform-conditional code, consistent with straightforward portability across JVM-hosting operating systems.

The JVM compilation target itself gives Kotlin the JVM's 'write once, run anywhere' bytecode portability across operating systems supporting a JVM (Linux, Windows, macOS), which is a strong platform-neutrality property inherited by language design choice.
Kotlin/Native and Kotlin/JS targets are separate compiler backends from the same frontend, meaning platform neutrality is a designed-in compiler architecture property, not an ecosystem afterthought.

Some standard library APIs differ slightly in availability across JVM/JS/Native (common vs. platform-specific stdlib subsets), which is a real but modest constraint on full platform neutrality at the API level.
